title: Electrochemistry
subject: Chemistry

blocks.text: An electrochemical cell is a device in which chemical energy is converted into electrical energy or electrical energy is used to bring about a chemical reaction. Electrochemical cells are classified into two types:

items: Galvanic cells (Voltaic cells): Convert chemical energy into electrical energy through a spontaneous redox reaction.
Electrolytic cells: Use electrical energy to bring about a non-spontaneous chemical reaction.

blocks.text: A redox reaction is a chemical reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.

items: Oxidation: Loss of electrons.
Reduction: Gain of electrons.

blocks.text: Zinc loses electrons, so it undergoes oxidation.
Copper ions gain electrons, so they undergo reduction.
Working Principle of an Electrochemical Cell

In a galvanic cell, oxidation and reduction occur at separate electrodes. The electrons released during oxidation travel through an external wire to the electrode where reduction occurs. This flow of electrons produces an electric current.

The two electrodes are connected through an external wire, while the electrolytic solutions are connected through a salt bridge in a conventional galvanic cell.

The main components are:

items: Anode: The electrode where oxidation takes place.
Cathode: The electrode where reduction takes place.
Electrolyte: A solution or molten substance containing mobile ions that conduct electricity.
Salt bridge: Connects the two half-cells and maintains electrical neutrality by allowing ions to migrate.

blocks.text: Illustration of a galvanic cell showing electrodes, salt bridge and electron flow.

items: Oxidation always occurs at the anode.
Reduction always occurs at the cathode.
In a galvanic cell, the anode is negative and the cathode is positive.
Electrons flow through the external circuit from the anode to the cathode.
Electric current in the external circuit flows in the opposite direction to electron flow.
The salt bridge completes the internal circuit and maintains electrical neutrality.

blocks.text: A galvanic cell is an electrochemical cell that converts the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy. A common example is the Daniell cell, which consists of a zinc electrode dipped in zinc sulphate solution and a copper electrode dipped in copper sulphate solution.
The Daniell cell consists of two half-cells:

items: Anode (Zinc electrode): A zinc rod dipped in \(\ce{ZnSO4}\) solution.
Cathode (Copper electrode): A copper rod dipped in \(\ce{CuSO4}\) solution.

blocks.text: The two solutions are connected by a salt bridge, and the electrodes are connected externally by a conducting wire.
Zinc loses two electrons and forms zinc ions. These electrons flow through the external wire towards the copper electrode.
Copper ions gain two electrons and are deposited as copper metal on the copper electrode.

Thus, zinc dissolves into the solution, while copper is deposited on the copper electrode.

The salt bridge usually contains an inert electrolyte such as \(\ce{KCl}\) or \(\ce{KNO3}\).

Its main functions are:

items: It completes the electrical circuit by allowing ions to migrate.
It maintains electrical neutrality in both half-cells.
It prevents direct mixing of the two electrolyte solutions.
It minimises the liquid junction potential.

blocks.text: Electrode potential is the potential difference developed between an electrode and the electrolyte in which it is dipped due to the tendency of the electrode to lose or gain electrons. For example, when a zinc rod is dipped in a solution containing \(\ce{Zn^2+}\) ions, some zinc atoms may enter the solution as ions, leaving electrons behind on the rod. This produces a potential difference between the electrode and the solution. Similarly, metal ions may gain electrons and get deposited on an electrode.
The standard electrode potential is the electrode potential measured under standard conditions:

items: Concentration of ions: \(1\text{ M}\)
Gas pressure: \(1\text{ bar}\)
Temperature: generally \(298\text{ K}\)

blocks.text: The electrode potential cannot be measured directly for a single electrode. It is measured relative to a reference electrode.
The Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) is used as the primary reference electrode for measuring electrode potentials. Its standard electrode potential is assigned a value of zero volts.
The standard hydrogen electrode consists of:

items: A platinum electrode coated with platinum black.
A solution containing hydrogen ions of concentration \(1\text{ M}\).
Pure hydrogen gas passed over the platinum electrode at a pressure of \(1\text{ bar}\).
A temperature of \(298\text{ K}\).

Conductance is the measure of the ease with which an electrical current passes through a conductor. It is the reciprocal of resistance.

items: \(G\) = conductance
\(R\) = resistance

notes.heading: 2.4.2 Variation of Conductivity and Molar Conductivity with Concentration (Kohlrausch's Law)

blocks.text: The conductivity and molar conductivity of an electrolyte change with its concentration. Their behaviour is different for strong and weak electrolytes.

Conductivity (\(\kappa\)) generally increases with increasing concentration because the number of ions present per unit volume increases.

On dilution, conductivity decreases because the number of ions per unit volume decreases.
2. Variation of Molar Conductivity with Concentration

Molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)) increases with dilution because the ions can move more freely, and the degree of ionisation may increase. The increase in molar conductivity is different for strong and weak electrolytes. Strong electrolytes: Strong electrolytes, such as \(\ce{NaCl}\) and \(\ce{KCl}\), ionise almost completely in solution. Their molar conductivity increases gradually on dilution because interionic attractions decrease, allowing ions to move more freely. Weak electrolytes: Weak electrolytes, such as \(\ce{CH3COOH}\), ionise only partially in solution. Their molar conductivity increases sharply on dilution because both ionic mobility and the degree of ionisation increase.

The molar conductivity at infinite dilution, when the concentration approaches zero, is called limiting molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m^\circ\)). At infinite dilution, the ions behave independently, and the influence of interionic attractions becomes negligible. For strong electrolytes, the variation of molar conductivity with concentration is approximately described by

An electrolytic cell is a device in which electrical energy is used to bring about a non-spontaneous chemical reaction. The process of using electrical energy to produce a chemical change in an electrolyte is called electrolysis. For example, when an electric current is passed through molten sodium chloride, it decomposes into sodium metal and chlorine gas.

items: Electrolyte: A molten ionic compound or an ionic solution that conducts electricity through mobile ions.
Anode: The electrode connected to the positive terminal of the external power source.
Cathode: The electrode connected to the negative terminal of the external power source.
Battery or power supply: Provides the electrical energy required for the chemical reaction.

blocks.text: When an electric current passes through the electrolyte:

items: Positively charged ions (cations) move towards the cathode and gain electrons. Hence, reduction occurs at the cathode.
Negatively charged ions (anions) move towards the anode and lose electrons. Hence, oxidation occurs at the anode.
Electrical energy drives the non-spontaneous chemical reaction.

blocks.text: Remember: Oxidation always occurs at the anode, and reduction always occurs at the cathode, regardless of the type of electrochemical cell.

blocks.text: A battery is a device consisting of one or more electrochemical cells that converts chemical energy into electrical energy. Batteries are widely used in mobile phones, watches, vehicles, calculators and other electronic devices. A battery operates through redox reactions. Oxidation occurs at the anode, and reduction occurs at the cathode, producing electrical energy.
Batteries are classified into two main types:

Primary batteries cannot be recharged easily because their chemical reactions are essentially irreversible under normal operating conditions. Once the reactants are consumed, the battery is discarded. Examples:

items: Dry cell
Mercury cell

blocks.text: Secondary batteries can be recharged by passing an external electric current through them. During charging, the chemical reactions are driven in the reverse direction, restoring the reactants. Examples:

items: Lead storage battery
Nickel-cadmium cell
It should provide a steady voltage for a reasonable period.
It should have a high energy density.
It should be safe, reliable and easy to use.
It should have a long service life.
It should be economical for its intended application.

blocks.text: The main difference between primary and secondary batteries is that primary batteries are generally used until their reactants are consumed, whereas secondary batteries can be recharged and reused.

notes.heading: 2.6.1 Primary Batteries (Dry Cell and Mercury Cell)

blocks.text: Primary batteries are electrochemical cells in which the chemical reactions are essentially irreversible under normal operating conditions. Therefore, they cannot be recharged easily and are generally discarded after use.
A dry cell is a primary battery commonly used in torches, wall clocks, remote controls and toys. Construction:

items: Anode: The zinc container acts as the negative electrode.
Cathode: A carbon rod surrounded by a mixture of manganese dioxide \(\ce{MnO2}\) and carbon powder.
Electrolyte: A moist paste containing ammonium chloride \(\ce{NH4Cl}\) and zinc chloride \(\ce{ZnCl2}\).

blocks.text: Working: Zinc undergoes oxidation and releases electrons.

At the cathode, manganese dioxide participates in the reduction process. The exact cathode chemistry depends on the electrolyte composition and operating conditions. The dry cell produces a voltage of approximately \(1.5\text{ V}\). Uses: Torches, clocks, remote controls and other low-power electronic devices.
A mercury cell is a primary battery that provides a nearly constant voltage during its useful life. It was traditionally used in watches, calculators and small electronic instruments. Construction:

items: Anode: Zinc amalgam.
Cathode: A mixture of mercury(II) oxide \(\ce{HgO}\) and carbon.
Electrolyte: Potassium hydroxide \(\ce{KOH}\) or sodium hydroxide \(\ce{NaOH}\).

blocks.text: Working: At the anode, zinc is oxidised:
At the cathode, mercury(II) oxide is reduced:

The mercury cell produces a nearly constant voltage of approximately \(1.35\text{ V}\). Uses: Traditionally used in watches, calculators and hearing aids. Its use has declined because mercury is toxic and environmentally hazardous.

notes.heading: 2.6.2 Secondary Batteries (Lead Storage Battery and Nickel-Cadmium Cell)

blocks.text: Secondary batteries are electrochemical cells that can be recharged by passing an external electric current through them. During charging, the chemical reactions are driven in the reverse direction, allowing the battery to be used repeatedly.
A lead storage battery is a rechargeable battery commonly used in automobiles and backup power systems. Construction:

items: Anode during discharge: Lead \(\ce{Pb}\).
Cathode during discharge: Lead dioxide \(\ce{PbO2}\).
Electrolyte: Aqueous sulphuric acid \(\ce{H2SO4}\).

At the cathode, lead dioxide is reduced:

During discharge, both electrodes are converted partly into lead sulphate, and the concentration of sulphuric acid decreases. Charging: When an external direct current is applied in the reverse direction, the reactions reverse, regenerating lead and lead dioxide and increasing the sulphuric acid concentration. Each lead storage cell produces approximately \(2\text{ V}\). Six cells connected in series provide approximately \(12\text{ V}\). Uses:

items: Automobile starting batteries
Inverters and emergency power supplies
Backup power systems

items: Negative electrode during discharge: Cadmium \(\ce{Cd}\).
Positive electrode during discharge: Nickel oxyhydroxide \(\ce{NiO(OH)}\).
Electrolyte: Aqueous potassium hydroxide \(\ce{KOH}\).

blocks.text: Working During Discharge At the negative electrode, cadmium is oxidised:
At the positive electrode, nickel oxyhydroxide is reduced:

items: Rechargeable emergency lighting
Some cordless tools
Certain industrial and backup applications

blocks.text: A fuel cell is an electrochemical cell that converts the chemical energy of a fuel and an oxidising agent directly into electrical energy. Unlike conventional batteries, fuel cells can continue to produce electricity as long as fuel and the oxidising agent are supplied continuously.
A hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell uses hydrogen as the fuel and oxygen as the oxidising agent. It produces electricity, with water as the overall reaction product.
The hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell consists of:

items: Anode: The electrode where hydrogen is oxidised.
Cathode: The electrode where oxygen is reduced.
Electrolyte: A medium that allows ions to move between the electrodes.
Fuel supply: Hydrogen is continuously supplied to the anode.
Oxidant supply: Oxygen is continuously supplied to the cathode.

blocks.text: Porous carbon electrodes with suitable catalysts are commonly used in the conventional alkaline hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.
In an alkaline hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, the electrode reactions are as follows. At the anode — Oxidation Hydrogen reacts with hydroxide ions to produce water and electrons.
At the cathode — Reduction Oxygen reacts with water and electrons to produce hydroxide ions.
The electrons released at the anode flow through an external circuit to the cathode, producing electrical energy.

items: They convert chemical energy directly into electrical energy.
They can operate continuously when fuel and oxygen are supplied.
Hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells produce water as the main reaction product.
They can have high energy-conversion efficiency.
They can be used where reliable electricity is required.
Spacecraft and space missions
Fuel-cell electric vehicles
Stationary electricity generation
Backup power systems

blocks.text: Important: A fuel cell differs from a conventional battery because its fuel and oxidising agent are supplied continuously from outside rather than being stored entirely within the cell.

Corrosion is the slow destruction of a metal due to its chemical or electrochemical reaction with its surroundings. A common example is the rusting of iron in the presence of oxygen and moisture. Other examples include the formation of a green coating on copper and the tarnishing of silver.
Corrosion of iron occurs through the formation of tiny anodic and cathodic regions on its surface in the presence of moisture.
Iron loses electrons and forms ferrous ions. Oxidation occurs at the anodic region.
In the presence of dissolved oxygen and water, oxygen is reduced in the cathodic region under neutral or alkaline conditions.
The ferrous ions react with hydroxide ions to form iron(II) hydroxide.

Iron(II) hydroxide is further oxidised by oxygen to form iron(III) hydroxide, which undergoes further changes to produce hydrated iron(III) oxide, commonly called rust. Rust is represented approximately as
Rust is porous and does not protect the underlying iron effectively. Therefore, corrosion can continue.

items: Moisture: The presence of water generally promotes corrosion.
Oxygen: Oxygen supports the cathodic reaction involved in rusting.
Electrolytes: Dissolved salts increase the conductivity of moisture and can accelerate corrosion.
Acidic conditions: Acids often increase the rate of corrosion of iron.
Contact with dissimilar metals: Electrical contact between different metals in the presence of an electrolyte can accelerate corrosion of the more active metal.
Painting: A paint coating prevents contact between the metal and its surroundings.
Oiling and greasing: These form a protective layer that reduces contact with moisture and oxygen.
Galvanisation: Iron is coated with zinc, which protects the iron from corrosion.
Electroplating: A thin layer of another metal, such as chromium or tin, is deposited on the surface.
Alloying: Corrosion-resistant alloys, such as stainless steel, are produced by combining iron with suitable elements, particularly chromium.
Cathodic protection: The metal to be protected is made the cathode by connecting it to a more reactive sacrificial metal, such as zinc or magnesium.
Increases the service life of metal structures and equipment.
Reduces maintenance and replacement costs.
Improves the safety of bridges, pipelines, vehicles and storage tanks.
Prevents material loss and damage caused by corrosion.

summary: Chapter 2 covers electrochemical cells, distinguishing between galvanic cells (which convert chemical energy of spontaneous redox reactions into electrical energy) and electrolytic cells (which use electrical energy to drive non-spontaneous reactions). It explains the Daniell cell, salt bridge functions, cell notation, standard electrode potential measured using the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE), and the Nernst equation along with its relationships to the equilibrium constant and Gibbs energy change. The chapter also details electrical conductance, conductivity, cell constant, molar conductivity, their variation with concentration for strong and weak electrolytes, and Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions. Finally, it examines electrolysis, Faraday's first and second laws, primary batteries (dry cell, mercury cell), secondary batteries (lead storage battery, nickel-cadmium cell), hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells, and the electrochemical mechanism and prevention of corrosion.

qa.q: What is the main difference between a galvanic cell and an electrolytic cell?
qa.a: A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy through a spontaneous redox reaction (with a negative anode and positive cathode), whereas an electrolytic cell uses electrical energy from an external power supply to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction (with a positive anode and negative cathode).

qa.q: What are the main functions of a salt bridge in a galvanic cell?
qa.a: A salt bridge completes the electrical circuit by allowing ions to migrate, maintains electrical neutrality in both half-cells, prevents direct mixing of the two electrolyte solutions, and minimises the liquid junction potential.

qa.q: How is a Daniell cell represented in standard cell notation?
qa.a: A Daniell cell is represented as \(\ce{Zn(s) | Zn^2+(aq) || Cu^2+(aq) | Cu(s)}\), where a single vertical line represents a phase boundary, a double vertical line represents the salt bridge, the anode is on the left, and the cathode is on the right.

qa.q: What is the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) and what is its standard potential?
qa.a: The Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) is the primary reference electrode consisting of a platinum electrode coated with platinum black dipped in \(1\text{ M } \ce{H+}\) solution with pure \(\ce{H2}\) gas at \(1\text{ bar}\) and \(298\text{ K}\). Its standard electrode potential is assigned as \(0.00\text{ V}\).

qa.q: Write the Nernst equation for a cell at 298 K.
qa.a: At 298 K, the Nernst equation is \(E_{\text{cell}} = E_{\text{cell}}^\circ - \frac{0.0591}{n} \log Q\), where \(n\) is the number of electrons transferred and \(Q\) is the reaction quotient.

qa.q: How is the standard cell potential related to the equilibrium constant and standard Gibbs energy change?
qa.a: At 298 K, \(\log K = \frac{n E_{\text{cell}}^\circ}{0.0591}\) and \(\Delta G^\circ = -nF E_{\text{cell}}^\circ = -2.303 RT \log K\). When \(E_{\text{cell}}^\circ > 0\), \(\Delta G^\circ < 0\) and \(K > 1\), meaning the reaction is spontaneous and favours products.
qa.section: 2.3.2 Electrochemical Cell and Gibbs Energy of the Reaction

qa.q: How do conductivity and molar conductivity vary with dilution?
qa.a: On dilution, conductivity (\(\kappa\)) decreases because the number of ions per unit volume decreases, whereas molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)) increases because ions move more freely and the degree of ionisation increases.
qa.section: 2.4.2 Variation of Conductivity and Molar Conductivity with Concentration (Kohlrausch's Law)

qa.q: State Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions.
qa.a: Kohlrausch's law states that at infinite dilution, each ion contributes independently to the total limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte, regardless of the nature of the other ion present: \(\Lambda_m^\circ = x\lambda_+^\circ + y\lambda_-^\circ\).
qa.section: 2.4.2 Variation of Conductivity and Molar Conductivity with Concentration (Kohlrausch's Law)

qa.q: State Faraday's first and second laws of electrolysis.
qa.a: Faraday's first law states that the mass of a substance deposited or liberated at an electrode is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed (\(m = ZIt = \frac{MIt}{nF}\)). Faraday's second law states that when the same quantity of electricity passes through different electrolytes, the masses deposited are proportional to their equivalent masses (\(\frac{m_1}{m_2} = \frac{E_1}{E_2}\)).

qa.q: Why does a mercury cell provide a constant voltage throughout its life unlike a dry cell?
qa.a: The overall reaction of a mercury cell (\(\ce{Zn + HgO -> ZnO + Hg}\)) does not involve any ion in solution whose concentration changes during operation, so it provides a nearly constant voltage of about 1.35 V.
qa.section: 2.6.1 Primary Batteries (Dry Cell and Mercury Cell)

qa.q: What is the overall cell reaction in a lead storage battery during discharge?
qa.a: During discharge, lead at the anode and lead dioxide at the cathode react with sulphuric acid to form lead sulphate and water: \(\ce{Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4 -> 2PbSO4 + 2H2O}\).
qa.section: 2.6.2 Secondary Batteries (Lead Storage Battery and Nickel-Cadmium Cell)

qa.q: What is a fuel cell and what are its main advantages?
qa.a: A fuel cell is an electrochemical cell that converts the chemical energy of a continuously supplied fuel (like \(\ce{H2}\)) and oxidant (like \(\ce{O2}\)) directly into electrical energy. It operates continuously, has high efficiency, and produces non-polluting water as the main product.

qa.q: What is corrosion and how is rusting of iron prevented?
qa.a: Corrosion is the slow destruction of a metal due to chemical or electrochemical reaction with its surroundings, such as the rusting of iron to form \(\ce{Fe2O3 \cdot xH2O}\). It is prevented by painting, oiling/greasing, galvanisation, electroplating, alloying, and cathodic protection.
